opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing I took from Carlos is that a paper should exist because it changes what people can actually do, not just because you have a result to report. He always pushed us to ask: who is going to use this, and what will be different for them after they read it? That sounds simple, but it really filters out a lot of work that's technically interesting but doesn't move anything.

He also cared a lot about the full story. It wasn't enough to have a clever idea. You had to understand the problem deeply, show why existing approaches fall short, and then make something that works end to end in the real world. That's part of why I came to see building systems and open-source tools as part of research. With something like XGBoost, the paper mattered, but what mattered more was that people could pick it up, run it on their data, and get value from it. Carlos encouraged that mindset. Impact was the goal, and the paper was one way to communicate it.

The other lesson was about taste. He would often say, in one way or another, that you should work on things that would still matter in a few years. So before writing, I ask myself whether the idea solves a real bottleneck, whether it's general enough that others can build on it, and whether I'd still be proud of it later. If the answer is yes, it's worth writing. If it's only incremental, it's probably better to keep pushing until it becomes something more meaningful.

fable-5.1.text:
Carlos had this way of asking a very simple question whenever you brought him an idea: who is going to use this, and what will they be able to do tomorrow that they couldn't do today? At first that felt almost unfair, because as a student you want to talk about the clever trick, the bound you proved, the architecture you found. But he would just keep steering back to the problem. He didn't care much whether something was fashionable. He cared whether it was real.

The thing that really shaped me was watching how he treated engineering. In a lot of places, building a system is seen as the thing you do after the research, almost like cleanup. Carlos treated it as part of the research. When we were working on XGBoost, it would have been easy to write it up as "gradient boosting with a few tweaks" and move on. He pushed me to think about why people would actually reach for it, what the scaling behavior meant for practitioners, and how to tell that story honestly. The paper came out of the tool being useful, not the other way around.

So my sense of what makes a paper worth writing became pretty concrete. It's worth writing if it changes what someone can build, or if it explains something that was confusing to many people in a way that sticks. If I can't say who benefits, that's a signal to go back and do more work before writing anything. I also learned from him that a paper is a form of communication, not a trophy. You write it so other people can pick up where you left off.

And he was generous in a way that mattered. He gave me a lot of room to go build things that didn't look like typical PhD output, and he trusted that the ideas would come out of that. That trust is something I try to pass on to my own students now.

astra-6.text:
What I took from Carlos was to start with the question, rather than with the goal of writing a paper. Is this a problem that matters? If we solve it, what will someone be able to do that they couldn’t do before? That changes how you choose projects, because an idea can be technically interesting without necessarily addressing an important need.

So, for me, a paper became a way to communicate something useful we had learned. The value wasn’t just in getting the paper accepted, but in whether the work gave other people something they could understand, use, and build on.

sol-6.1.text:
What I learned from Carlos was to start with the question: is this a problem that really matters? You can have a technically interesting idea, but you also need to understand why someone would care about the result and what it would enable them to do.

That shaped how I think about systems research. A paper is an opportunity to communicate an insight, and the system you build is a way to test whether that insight holds up in practice. So rather than starting with, “How do we get a paper out of this?” I try to ask, “What are we learning, and could that learning be useful beyond this particular implementation?”
